detail.abstract: The illegal killing of Cecil the Lion in 2015 crystalized public disapproval of the trophy hunting of endangered species. Hunting endangered species was not initially supported by two major moral philosophies concerning wildlife: Animal Rights / Utilitarianism, and Environmental Ethicists. Varner (1998) shows that these philosophies can converge for some forms of therapeutic hunting such as reducing overpopulation. We show that whether our obligations to animals are to maximize their aggregate welfare (Singer (1995)), or to protect and promote their rights (Regan (2004)), or to secure the integrity and stability of their ecosystem (Leopold (2001) and Callicott (1989)), Sports Trophy hunting can be moral permissible, and arguably morally obligated under three necessary conditions. These are: 1) the conservation of the endangered species is of high moral importance and urgency, 2) a hunting program, perhaps jointly with other efforts, reliably causes a significant conservation effect, and 3) there are no feasible, ready-to-hand alternatives to hunting that would achieve even a close-to-comparable conservation effect on the hunted species. These conditions could form a base for future regulation. A successful case study is presented for the Kashmir Markhor on the border of Afghanistan and Pakistan.

title: Rethinking Africa's Dependency Paradigm: Industrial Development as the Pathway to Economic Sovereignty and Employment Creation

detail.title: Rethinking Africa's Dependency Paradigm: Industrial Development as the Pathway to Economic Sovereignty and Employment Creation
detail.abstract: For over six decades, African economies have remained embedded in an external dependency structure characterized by the export of raw materials and the import of manufactured goods. Despite successive development strategies, this pattern has persisted, constraining structural transformation and perpetuating unemployment. The growing dominance of digital economies, geopolitical realignments, and the green transition underscore the urgency of rethinking Africa's growth model. This paper argues that Africa's economic sovereignty and employment generation depend on transitioning from an extractive dependency model to an inclusive industrial development paradigm. Drawing on dependency and endogenous growth theories, it explores how regional value chains, SME-driven manufacturing, and digital financial inclusion can catalyze industrial learning, productivity, and sustainable job creation. The study concludes that Africa's path to self-determined prosperity lies not in aiddependence or commodity exportation but in nurturing endogenous capacity for production, innovation, and technological diffusion.

detail.title: Rethinking the economics curriculum: strengths and weaknesses of the CORE Econ project
detail.abstract: The Global Financial Crisis of 2007–2008 exposed the economics profession’s limited ability to forecast or effectively use the theoretical frameworks being taught in universities to explain it. This failure resulted in a widespread distrust in the profession and sparked a wave of student protests worldwide, demanding improvements to the mainstream economics curriculum. In response, a group of academics led by Sam Bowles and Wendy Carlin initiated the CORE Econ project in 2013, aiming to develop a new benchmark for teaching introductory economics. Within a year, the team released a freely available online eBook called The Economy, marking the beginning of a growing and ongoing project. This paper traces the evolution of the CORE Econ project over the years, highlighting its primary advantages and criticisms that might be levelled against it. Regardless of one’s stance as a supporter or sceptic, it is evident that the CORE Econ approach has had a profound impact, leaving a lasting mark on the publishing and economics education landscape.

detail.title: Impacts of Communication and Dot Plots on Interest Rates: the Case of Korea

publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Korea Economic Research Institute Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This study examines the impact of forward guidance on short- and long-term interest rates in Korea, focusing on the effectiveness of Bank of Korea’s dot plots in shaping market expectations. Using an econometric model, we analyze how forward guidance through press conferences (communication shocks) and providing Monetary Policy Board (MPB) members’ base rates expectations (dot plots) after the MPB meetings influence various interest rates across different maturities. The results show that the dot plot shock amplifies communication effects, impacting both short-term and long-term interest rates. Notably, it has a more direct effect on bonds with maturities of three months or less, aligning with the dot plot’s targeted timeframe. In contrast, the conventional monetary policy shock is shown to influence only short-term interest rates. These findings suggest that the MPB effectively manages both short- and long-term market expectations through forward guidance while preserving flexibility for future policy adjustments.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how IOs’ vision and policy priorities for the future of development and education have evolved across time, focusing on three global crises: the Sputnik Crisis in 1957; the oil crises of the 1970s; and the global financial crisis in 2008-2009. It also explores IOs' historical socio-material futuring practices employed to promote their visions from their inception up to the 2010s, illustrating the entanglements of policy networks and events, results-based development aid infrastructure, and representational technologies. Through these examinations, this paper demonstrates how IOs had competed over the vision of redistributive and liberal development and education with the seemingly common global agenda - such as manpower and education planning during the 1960s, partnerships during the 1970s, Education for All during the 1990s, Millenium Development Goals during the 2000s, and Sustainable Development Goals for the 2010s. The finding of this study shows the politics of crisis time illustrated in IOs' repetitive struggles for envisioning endogenous versus aided development and skills versus lifelong education in defining the predominant visions of international development and education. Having gone through key global crises over the course of 70 years, particular stories and socio-technical imaginaries for neoliberal globalization have been reinforced through IOs’ socio-material practices. There has been a continuity in seeking rational development goals in the pursuit of modernity resulting in the current predominance of the SDGs and global aid and education data infrastructures which locate us within a monitoring movement across all three IOs. While UNESCO has been beset by international relations from the onset of the Cold War, the OECD and the World Bank have risen to the global leadership in international development and education, resourced with member states' stable funding and buoyed by their mission of economic modernization and neoliberal globalization. The repetitive silences and disadvantages followed by development initiatives illustrate the politics and power relations reinforced by international development and education despite the seemingly rationalistic story, technical infrastructures, and cooperative practices.

detail.abstract: This study examines the evolving legal architecture concerning AI-generated evidence. It focuses on the varied approaches of the European Union and India regarding its admissibility in criminal proceedings. Open-box AI evidence refers to transparent AI systems whose decision-making processes are interpretable. This allows stakeholders to understand the reasoning behind automated outputs. The importance of this study lies in the increasing reliance on AI systems in law; particularly in high-stakes environments. This necessitates a robust regulatory environment to protect fundamental rights and ensure the integrity of evidence. A notable lacuna exists in the harmonization of standards for AI-generated evidence across jurisdictions. The principal objective of this paper is to delineate key regulatory elements plus proffer actionable recommendations for India by leveraging insights from the EU's comprehensive approach. This particularly involves the EU AI Act and the General Data Protection Regulation. The methodology involves a comparative analysis of legal texts and various regulatory provisions. Alongside, it involves qualitative assessments of techno-ethical standards. Key findings elucidate that the EU has established robust regulatory measures. Whereas India is in the incipient stages of developing a coherent framework. Preliminary results suggest that adopting a risk-based taxonomy for AI systems, accompanied by unequivocal criteria for reliability can enhance the legal framework in India. The implications of this research are substantial, as the establishment of a robust regulatory schema can fortify public trust in AI tech. It can also facilitate transnational co-operation. The study aims to contribute to the discourse on AI in law. It offers promising results that advocate for a judicious equilibrium in the adoption of technology within criminal justice system.

detail.abstract: This paper weighs in on a heavy topic: Argentina's financial tails are the fattest in the Western Hemisphere. With excess kurtosis of 36.3, the Merval is not just an outlierit's an out-liar, consistently telling risk models things that turn out to be false. A single trading day (August 12, 2019) produced a-37.9% return, which under Gaussian assumptions is less likely than finding a honest politician in the Congreso. I document that standard risk models underestimate Argentine tail risk by a factor of 4-6, meaning your VaR is really just a VAR: a Vaguely Accurate Rumor. The practical implication is clear: anyone using normal distributions for Argentine assets is distributing their capital normally-that is, to other people.

detail.abstract: This paper will analyze the law that governs censorship of the judiciary and the media in Pakistan. It examines how Article 19 of the constitution ensures the right to free speech is tensioned with legal tools to suppress it, including the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (PECA) 2016, the contempt of court laws, or laws of general media. The study contends that although judicial censorship, practiced by involving the exercise of the suo moto power and contempt citation, is supposed to safeguard institutional power and national interest, it tends to limit judicial responsibility and press freedom. At the same time, the censorship of media, which is imposed either by state institutions or by coercion, subverts democratic discourse. The results suggest that this twofold censorship results in a complicated scenario of free expression where the judiciary will be both a possible protector of the rights and a restrictive force. The paper finds that legal provisions must be rebalanced between the dignity of the judiciary and the basic liberties by recalibration of the law.

detail.abstract: The global economy is not currently structured to support decision-making or allocating financial resources in a way that consistently accounts for the interrelationships between biodiversity, water, food, health and climate change or their connections to human well-being and the economy. The financial system – including public, private, domestic and international institutions like banks, insurance companies and stock exchanges – plays an important role in helping to direct financial resources towards their most productive uses, channelling funds from where surpluses are generated to where there are shortfalls in ways which reduce transactions costs and manage risks (Schoenmaker et al., 2012). Critically, however, what appears as productive uses of financial resources within the financial system in fact depends on the information that is considered in allocating resources and the enabling environment in which an investment is taking place; thus, responding to signals provided only by markets can lead to a significant misallocation of resources (Dasgupta, 2021b). Likewise, the hypothesis that financial markets can efficiently allocate resources assumes that financial markets are equally developed around the world, which is not the case, and means that access to affordable finance for investments can be a significant problem in lower income countries (Schoenmaker & Volz, 2022).

title: The Stayed Stream: A Critical Analysis of Juristic Personhood for the River Ganga – Drowning in Legalese

detail.title: The Stayed Stream: A Critical Analysis of Juristic Personhood for the River Ganga – Drowning in Legalese
detail.abstract:
This paper engages with the recent innovation of applying juristic personhood to the River Ganga as a remedy for its severe environmental degradation. In the landmark case of Mohd. Salim v. State of Uttarakhand in 2017, the Uttarakhand High Court held that the Ganga and its major tributary, the Yamuna, are "living entities," upon which the full contingent of rights, duties, and liabilities of a juristic person were conferred. This is a landmark decision in Indian environmental law because it departs from the norm of regulatory controls, which had proven inadequate to protect one of India's most sacred ecological systems from catastrophic pollution.

The High Court initially utilized borrowed principle of parens patriae, drawing upon existing precedents where non-humans, including corporate bodies and sacred symbols like idols, have been juristic persons. Though the impetus behind establishing the idea of personhood for the river was ultimately to provide legal immunity for action on behalf of the river and its ecosystems, it does establish new legal standing for the rivers' personhood which made it possible to utilize the courts in managing change to protect and maintain health and ecological integrity for rivers. The High Court appointed public officers to act in loco parentis, effectively as servants of the court appointed with obligations of care to protect the rivers.

But despite this momentous ruling, the recognition of these rights was both celebrated and condemned and ultimately was stayed by the Supreme Court of India. Criticisms cited certain problems of practicality and legality, such as, the question of the non-specific nature of the powers and duties of the rivers, the potential of legal entanglement between riparian states; and the absurdity of appointing public servants as one of the chief guardians of the rivers, considering their administrations oversaw their respective rivers' deterioration. Moreover, academics and activists have argued that any form of rights-based system would only be effective if there was an apparent enforcement mechanism or, at a minimum, a clear community-based management component that emphasised community-based stewardship, such as the New Zealand Whanganui River regulatory scheme, rather than relying solely on state actors.

I argue that while the Uttarakhand High Court's decision was a strong symbolic and jurisprudential step towards an ecocentric legal paradigm, the application of its decision was riddled with unenforced regional ambiguities. I have constructed my mode of inquiry by organising the paper into five sections. Firstly, I shall begin by outlining the ecological importance of river Ganga and its cultural sanctity in India, that accorded it the significance it currently enjoys. Secondly, I detail the landmark case of Mohd. Salim v. State of Uttarakhand, 2017, describing the reasoning that led to the Uttarakhand High Court passing the order declaring Ganga as a juristic person. Thirdly, I will attempt to analyse a cause-and-effect relationship between granting such status and the impact it holds for natural persons vis-à-vis the juristic person i.e., Ganga. Fourthly, I will describe the potential ramifications due to the ambiguity of the judgment and the challenges that need to be addressed. Lastly, I will provide suggestive reforms to address these ambiguities and challenges to provide a convalescing recovery to the Ganga.

title: “CHINAS”: Chinese Household Inflation-Linked National Annuity-Linked Securities
affiliations: Georgetown University and Georgetown University - McDonough School of Business

detail.title: “CHINAS”: Chinese Household Inflation-Linked National Annuity-Linked Securities
detail.abstract: China’s population aging has become an increasingly urgent challenge, placing severe pressure on its fiscal system, labor market, and, most critically, the sustainability of its pension system. Despite ongoing reforms, the outlook for China’s basic pension remains grim as declining fertility, high youth unemployment, and growing local fiscal distress undermine the foundation of its Pay-as-You-Go (PAYG) structure. To address these challenges, this paper proposes CHINAS (Chinese Household Inflation-linked National Annuity Securities) — a new class of simple, low-cost, low-risk, digitally enabled, government-issued bonds designed to transform individual retirement savings. Modeled after Merton and Muralidhar’s (2020) SeLFIES, CHINAS integrates accumulation, decumulation, compounding, and inflation protection within a single transparent instrument. Each bond pays ¥10 (real) per month for 15 years after retirement, indexed to Value-Added Tax (VAT) to hedge inflation and maintain purchasing power. Accessible via digital payment platforms such as Alipay and WeChat Pay, CHINAS can be purchased in small denominations, promoting financial inclusion and nationwide participation. The proposal represents a win-win-win for citizens, the government, and the financial sector — making retirement savings simple, sustainable, and secure for future generations.

detail.abstract: The key issue addressed in this paper is the complexity of establishing national criminal jurisdiction over cybercrimes, the elements of which may be scattered across different countries. The author examines how different states adapt or create special jurisdictional norms to cover such acts, using the "effect doctrine" or expanding the protective principle, as well as implementing modern achievements in the theory of conflict of criminal laws into legislation without resorting to casuistry. The conclusion is made that for Russia, a more preferable path is to modernize existing legislative approaches, considering the scientific understanding of the phenomenon of establishing jurisdiction, rather than creating special norms.

title: Enhancing Driving Risk Scores with Near-Miss Events: Evidence from Electric-Vehicle Telematics
affiliations: Southwestern University of Finance and Economics, University of Hawaii at Manoa and Southwestern University of Finance and Economics

detail.title: Enhancing Driving Risk Scores with Near-Miss Events: Evidence from Electric-Vehicle Telematics
detail.abstract: Near-miss events-incidents in which a crash nearly occurs-provide frequent, behaviorally rich signals about driving risk that claims alone cannot capture. We propose a two-stage framework that leverages this information by integrating the full predictive distribution of near-miss events into the claim probability function. The first stage estimates the conditional claim probability given near-miss occurrences and telematics features; the second stage predicts the distribution of near-miss counts. Combining these components via the Law of Total Probability yields a posterior-like claim probability that reflects both behavioral patterns and uncertainty in near-miss occurrences. These probabilities are then calibrated and transformed into interpretable driving risk scores suitable for insurers, fleet operators, and mobility platforms. We evaluate this framework using a large telematics dataset of 1,300 electric vehicles (EVs) from China. EVs differ from internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles in key aspects such as power delivery, battery dynamics, and regenerative braking. Granular Battery Management System (BMS) data, capturing state of charge, voltage, current, temperature, and cell anomalies, provides EV-specific information that enrichs behavioral and operational risk assessment beyond what conventional telematics can offer. Using both generalized linear models (GLMs) and tree-based machine learning models, we show that the proposed two-stage approach substantially improves claim prediction and risk discrimination. In the test sample, the highest-risk quintile based on the two-stage model captures 56% of claims, compared with 40% under a naïve two-stage model using mean near-miss counts and only 17% under a one-stage model using observed counts. Similar improvements hold when using conventional telematics alone, indicating the possibility of applying our model to ICE vehicles as well. Additional analysis reveals that tree-based models significantly outperform GLM alternatives and that EV-specific features meaningfully enhance predictive accuracy.

detail.abstract: Hybrid intelligence research emphasizes the importance of combining human and artificial intelligence, yet it lacks concrete cognitive architectures that specify how shared reasoning, control, and accountability are organized in practice. This paper introduces BALLERINA, a human-centered hybrid intelligence architecture that structures human-AI collaboration through explicit role separation, constraint, and justification loops. Rather than treating AI as an autonomous agent or social peer, BALLERINA formalizes complementary functions in which humans retain interpretive and ethical authority while the AI stabilizes reasoning, enforces constraints, and surfaces justification failures. By defining the human-AI ensemble as a sociotechnical reasoning system, this work provides an architectural foundation for hybrid intelligence that precedes empirical evaluation.

title: The Core Structure of Stoic Ethics: Control, Judgment, and Inner Freedom

detail.title: The Core Structure of Stoic Ethics: Control, Judgment, and Inner Freedom
detail.abstract: This article reconstructs Stoic ethics as a coherent system of practical reason structured around three functionally interconnected elements: the distinction between what lies within human control and what does not, the central role of judgment as the locus of moral responsibility, and inner freedom as the proper goal of Stoic practice. It responds to contemporary popularizations of Stoicism that reduce the tradition to motivational rhetoric, emotional self-control, or techniques of resilience and self-optimization. Against these reductions, the article argues that Stoic philosophy does not aim at behavioural regulation or the suppression of emotions, but at the clarification of inner evaluations. Within the Stoic framework, affects are understood as consequences of judgments rather than primary causes of suffering. Ethical responsibility is therefore strictly limited to the domain of assent and evaluation. Inner freedom emerges from the consistent decoupling of moral value from external circumstances and outcomes. By systematically linking control, judgment, and freedom, Stoicism appears as a normative model of inner sovereignty that resists instrumentalization while remaining relevant to contemporary ethical and leadership discourses. The article presents Stoic ethics as a demanding yet realistic framework for responsible self-governance in a contingent world. This reconstruction does not aim at an exhaustive engagement with contemporary exegetical debates, but at a systematic clarification of the internal ethical structure of Stoicism as a model of practical reason.

title: Quality Case Study Analysis: Nike Inc.

detail.title: Quality Case Study Analysis: Nike Inc.
detail.abstract: This case study analyzes the quality management practices of Nike Inc., focusing on the challenges created by manufacturing defects and global supply chain inconsistencies. Using Total Quality Management (TQM), Quality Management Systems (QMS), and Kaizen as analytical frameworks, the study evaluates how gaps in supplier oversight, inconsistent production standards, and rising defect rates have affected product quality, customer satisfaction, and brand reputation. A mixed-method approach combining case review, performance data analysis, and stakeholder insights reveals significant variability in product quality across Nike’s international supplier network. The study further assesses the effectiveness of Nike’s recent quality initiatives, including strengthened supplier audits, QMS enhancements, and continuous improvement programs. While these interventions have improved product consistency and operational efficiency, persistent supply chain complexity continues to pose quality risks. The paper concludes with strategic recommendations such as expanding Kaizen adoption, digitizing quality systems through predictive analytics, and investing in supplier development to ensure long-term, globally consistent quality excellence.

detail.title: Finnish Standardization Panel Pilot Study: Preliminary Observations and a Research Agenda
detail.abstract: Standardization ecosystems are arguably inseparable components of innovation ecosystems and national innovation systems. The design of standardization institutions may impact innovation incentives, appropriation of research and development investments and the rate and direction of technological progress. We evaluate the status of the Finnish standardization ecosystem and the role of standardization for the stakeholders of the Finnish standardization ecosystem. Extensive stakeholder interviews provided diverse perspectives of which the following saturated observations can be highlighted. First, the role and impacts of standards vary across industries, so the perspectives on the functioning of standardization systems vary accordingly. Second, standardization education is not systematic in Finland, indicating that standardization education could be improved to complement the learning by doing approach in organizations. Third, the role of standardization is expected to increase in the future, but geopolitical tensions cast a shadow on the functioning of the system. The pilot study provides one benchmark for the analysis of national standardization ecosystems in other (European) small open economies. We conclude by presenting a research agenda.

title: When Experience Waits: The Economics of Strategic Decline in Franchise Contracts

detail.title: When Experience Waits: The Economics of Strategic Decline in Franchise Contracts
detail.abstract: This paper studies strategic decline in franchise systems, a setting in which experienced franchisees optimally delay acceptance of new contracts in anticipation of acquiring them later through resale following newcomer failure. I develop a dynamic model with Bayesian learning and resale markets in which contract terms shape both operating incentives and the option value of waiting. Strategic decline arises endogenously from standard franchise fees and royalty rates and distorts the timing and allocation of contracts. I characterize the resulting efficiency losses and show that revenue-maximizing contracts need not minimize inefficiency. The analysis further derives contract designs (i.e., dynamic, discriminatory) that mitigate strategic delay by aligning acceptance incentives with learning and failure risk. Together, the results provide a unified framework for understanding how learning, resale frictions, and contract design interact to shape efficiency in franchise systems.

declarations.funderStatement: ANII, FCEA

detail.abstract: The objective of this is to analyse th links between Information Communication Technologies (ICTs), productivity, and exports at the micro level. To this end we use data from the Annual Economic Activity Survey (EAAE), to build a firm-level index of ICTs adoption for Uruguayan firms over the period 2012-2019, based on a Principal Components Analysis of detailed ICTs indicators. In a second step, a robust measure of Total Factor Productivity (TFP) is obtained for the same firms. These variables are then embedded in a three-equation Simultaneous Equations Model (SEMs) that jointly determines ICTs adoption, TFP and (log) exports, controlling for firm characteristics, industry level competition and fixed effects by year. Thus, we quantify within a single empirical framework, the feedback between digital technologies and productivity, and their joint impact on firms' export. Finally, we discriminate between manufacturing and services firm and compare the results. The baseline results for the full sample reveal a strong and statistically significant bidirectional relationship between ICTs and TFP: more productive firms tend to adopt more digital technologies, while higher ICTs adoption is associated with sizable gains in productivity. Both dimensions, in turn, exert large and economically meaningful effects on exports, with ICTs contributing directly to export performance and indirectly through productivity. When the model is re-estimated separately for manufacturing and service firms, the same qualitative patterns hold, but the intensities differ: the impact of TFP on ICTs adoption is somewhat stronger in manufacturing, whereas the effects of ICTs on TFP and on exports are relatively larger in services. These findings suggest that productivity is a general determinant of external competitiveness, while digital technologies are particularly critical for the internationalisation of service firms.

detail.abstract: I use an optimal contracting framework to address mixed empirical evidence on the impact of organizational higher purpose pursuit on the firm’s financial performance. Some empirical papers show that the authentic pursuit of a purpose that transcends the usual profit maximization goal leads to higher profits, which is theoretically puzzling since the pursuit of purpose often involves financial sacrifice (or else all firms would do it). Other papers show that the pursuit of purpose-driven initiatives can diminish firm profits. I develop a theoretical model in which there are firms that are purpose driven and those that are not, but all firms are observationally indistinguishable a priori. All employees are purpose-driven. Employees provide labor, motivated by optimal wage contracts designed by firms that provide capital. The model generates the following results: (1) Both the utility that employees attach to the pursuit of organizational higher purpose and the utility some firms attach to it lead to higher employee effort, but when the identities of firms are shrouded and the equilibrium is pooling in employee wages, the pure profit maximizers always do better financially. I also identify conditions under which purpose-driven firms do better financially than pure profit maximizers in a separating equilibrium. (2) When the equilibrium is separating in wages, purpose-driven firms pay higher wages than what they pay in a pooling equilibrium, but purpose-driven firms may pay higher or lower wages than pure profit maximizers in a separating equilibrium. (3) A separating equilibrium generates higher expected pecuniary output as well as a higher sum of pecuniary payoffs and purpose-linked utilities than a pooling equilibrium, but a sufficiently high social stigma associated with not being purpose-driven can induce firms to invest in shrouding their identities, generating inefficiencies. (4) Strengthening corporate governance designed to serve shareholders can lead to higher productive effort by purpose-driven employees.

detail.abstract: The article presents the results of the Russian adaptation of a short version of «PERMA+4 Employee Subjective Well-being Scale», developed in USA in 2020 on the basis of the Martin Seligman’s PERMA model (Positive emotions, Engagement, Relationships, Meaning, Accomplishment). This research is supposed to cover the lack of Russian-language psychometric instruments designed for theoretical study and practical assessment of the level of work-related subjective well-being. Translation and adaptation of the questionnaire were carried out in several stages taking into account modern international recommendations. The psychometric properties of the adapted questionnaire were tested on a sample of 325 company employees (average age — 43 years, 62% — women) from most economy sectors and regions of Russia. Content validity was tested with Subjective Well-Being Scale and Maslach Burnout Inventory, current validity — with Professional Motivation Questionnaire. The internal consistency was assessed by Cronbach's alpha and MacDonald's omega coefficients, the factor structure — by CFA and IRT methods. The factor structure was also tested on control sample (N=155). The adapted questionnaire showed acceptable validity, reliability (α = .83; ω = .88) and factor structure on the Primary (CFI = .9708; RMSEA = .0802; SRMR = .0342) and Control (CFI = .9703; RMSEA = .0797; SRMR = .0375) samples. Psychometric properties of the Russian version of PERMA+4 confirm the correctness of its translation and adaptation. The results suggest that the adapted short version of PERMA+4 is a sufficiently reliable instrument that can be used in future studies.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the impact of climate policy uncertainty (CPU) on green stock and crude oil returns using a causality-in-quantile test and a novel wavelet-based time-varying parametric quantile regression (WTPV-QR). We find that CPU is a Granger cause of both green stocks and crude oil returns across all quantiles. The effects are asymmetric and heterogeneous, particularly in extreme markets, and vary across time and frequency scales. Notably, the onset of the Russia-Ukraine war amplified these impacts. Moreover, CPU generally has a stronger effect on crude oil returns than on green stock returns under extreme market conditions. Finally, the short-term impacts of CPU exceed the long-term effects.

title: High-Performance Reservoir Simulation with Wafer-Scale Engine for Large-Scale Carbon Storage

detail.title: High-Performance Reservoir Simulation with Wafer-Scale Engine for Large-Scale Carbon Storage
detail.abstract: Reservoir simulations are essential for subsurface energy applications, but remain constrained by the long runtimes of high-fidelity solvers and the limited generalizability of pretrained machine learning models. This study presents a multiphase reservoir simulator implemented on the Wafer Scale Engine (WSE), a new hardware architecture that delivers supercomputer performance on a single chip. Application development on the WSE is still at a nascent stage, and this study is, to our knowledge, the first to implement a full-physics, two-phase CO2-brine reservoir simulator on WSE, achieving runtimes on the order of seconds for reservoir-scale simulations while preserving full numerical accuracy. The developed simulator incorporates detailed physics for simulating CO2 transport in geological formations. As a case study, we considered CO2 injection into a field-scale reservoir model consisting of over 1.7 million cells. The WSE solver achieves more than two orders of magnitude speedup compared to a conventional CPU-based parallel simulator, completing a 5-year simulation in just 2.8 s. The WSE performance remained nearly unchanged to a four-fold increase in grid resolution, in contrast to the strong slowdown observed with the CPU-based solver. These findings provide the first proof-of-concept of wafer-scale computing for enabling high-resolution, large-scale full-physics simulations in near-real-time, overcoming the tradeoff between speed and accuracy and opening a new paradigm for carbon storage and broader subsurface energy applications.

detail.abstract: Why do artists and other creators organize their work so differently, some acting as firms that integrate production and distribution, while others operate as contractors or salaried employees? We develop a framework in which creators choose how to organize the realization of their work, balancing coordination costs against the ability to appropriate returns when property rights and contracts are incomplete. These organizational choices correspond to alternative labor market arrangements-employment, contracting, and self-integration-that differ in autonomy, control, and exposure to imperfect appropriation. We apply the framework to Western classical music, where composers ranged from salaried employees under patronage (e.g., Bach, Haydn), to entrepreneurial freelancers who organized their own performances and publications under weak copyright (e.g., Mozart, Beethoven), to specialists who relied on publishers and orchestras once copyright and professional intermediation matured (e.g., Brahms, Tchaikovsky). The historical evolution from hierarchical employment to freelance contracting and selective self-production shows how technological, legal, and market conditions reshaped the organization of artistic labor. These same forces continue to shape creative labor today as digital platforms and AI again blur the boundaries between creators and intermediaries.

title: Why 95% of Papers in Top-Tier SCI Journals Are Garbage: A Critical Analysis of Academic Publishing Collapse

detail.title: Why 95% of Papers in Top-Tier SCI Journals Are Garbage: A Critical Analysis of Academic Publishing Collapse
detail.abstract: This paper presents a systematic analysis of why the overwhelming majority of publications in toptier SCI journals constitute low-quality or erroneous research that contributes minimally to genuine scientific progress. We establish a rigorous framework distinguishing garbage paper from genuinely valuable research, arguing that papers lacking theoretical advancement despite conducting real experiments represent the predominant publication category. The paper demonstrates that this garbage proliferation results not from individual researcher incompetence but from systematically perverse institutional incentives that reward publication volume, mainstream conformity, and resource consumption regardless of theoretical contribution. We document how PhD production requirements drive factories of meaningless empirical accumulation, how limited research resources are catastrophically misallocated to garbage papers, and how these waste-producing papers consume real societal resources through actual experimental implementation. Critically, we argue that the academic system deliberately suppresses acknowledgment of this crisis because identifying garbage papers as the statistical norm threatens the legitimacy of SCI journals, undermines publication incentive systems benefiting all participants, and challenges the authority of researchers who built careers on such work. We conclude that this is precisely why the problem must be articulated: the suppression of discussion about systemic garbage production reveals that garbage papers represent not a peripheral issue but the central dysfunction of modern academic publishing.

detail.abstract:
Fiscal Geometry is a tax-origin institutional framework that maps rule-triggered fiscal events on a two-axis plane: horizontal cross-jurisdictional fiscal shift and vertical intergenerational post-tax capacity. This paper tests whether that geometry remains coherent outside its original tax domain by using the 2008 global financial crisis as an extreme stress case.

Rather than retelling the crisis through price cycles, leverage narratives, or institutional blame, I reconstruct a stylized sequence of fiscal events as movements and rotations on the X–Y plane. Mortgage origination, securitization, and cross-market risk transfer are treated as lateral boundary-crossing events, while default cascades and balance-sheet compression are treated as vertical settlement dynamics. On this basis, I outline how a hypothetical tension index (ITI/gITI) could be formulated as a visibility instrument to track rising structural strain as flows concentrate toward critical thresholds.

The contribution of this paper is methodological: it defines an observational boundary for institutional analysis and illustrates how event-geometry can render systemic tension legible without claiming ex-ante forecasting accuracy or assigning responsibility.

title: A Fuzzy Logic Approach to Strategic Decision-Making Under Uncertainty
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: A Fuzzy Logic Approach to Strategic Decision-Making Under Uncertainty
detail.abstract: Strategic decisions are inherently difficult because they are defined by a high degree of complexity, incomplete information, and the inevitable influence of subjective judgment. Standard decisionmaking models, which rely on rigid binary logic, simply can't capture the subtle, "fuzzy" distinctions within concepts that are vital to strategy, such as judging a "high market potential" or assessing a "strong competitive rivalry." This paper introduces a conceptual framework designed to integrate fuzzy logic directly into the process of strategic decision-making under uncertainty. Our core argument is that fuzzy logic is a more natural and powerful tool for strategic analysis, primarily because of its unique ability to handle linguistic variables and measure the gradual belonging of an element to a set. This makes it ideal for modelling the genuine imprecision inherent in strategy. We lay out a clear, step-by-step methodology: first, identifying the key linguistic variables (like 'Competitive Intensity' and 'Internal Capability') and defining their membership functions; second, building a fuzzy rule base that logically captures expert strategic thinking; and finally, defuzzifying the resulting output to generate a clear, actionable strategic recommendation. To illustrate its utility, we provide a practical example focusing on a market entry strategy. This proposed framework gives managers a transparent and computationally sound method for organizing and analyzing complicated strategic problems, ultimately leading to decisions that are not only better but also easier to justify.

title: Rethinking AI Adoption for Frontier Markets

detail.abstract: Prevailing assessments of artificial-intelligence (AI) readiness in low-income and lower-middle-income economies (LLMICs) continue to rely predominantly on diffusion-level indicators-including individual awareness, platform interaction, and nominal connectivity-when evaluating prospective developmental benefit. While these metrics illuminate cross-national disparities in adoption, they insufficiently capture the mechanisms by which technological affordances are converted into macro-and meso-level welfare gains in structurally constrained environments. This paper advances Minimum-Effective-Diffusion (MED) as an alternative explanatory construct: a threshold-based model positing that marginal social benefit is maximized when AI and adjacent digital services are adopted and embedded by a limited but strategically central set of institutional actors, irrespective of broad population uptake. Drawing on empirical regularities across broadband penetration, digital-payment systems, mobile-money ecosystems, GovTech deployments, digital identity infrastructures, agricultural information services, and telehealth interventions—supplemented by analogs from electrification and modern-energy-minimum literature—we demonstrate that macroeconomic returns and welfare improvements frequently arise at sub-majority adoption levels. For example, mobile-money diffusion in Kenya yielded measurable poverty reductions at ~20–40% uptake, and incremental increases in digital-payment utilization exhibit proportionally larger elasticity with respect to GDP per capita than equivalent broadband-coverage expansion. These findings imply that institutionally mediated, workflow-integrated utilization—rather than diffuse, atomized consumer adoption—constitutes the primary channel through which early AI-complementary technologies propagate benefit in frontier-market contexts.Operationally, MED specifies three necessary components: (i) targeting institutional nodes (e.g., municipal administrations, health systems, agricultural cooperatives, SMEs) with procedural authority; (ii) strengthening service-layer infrastructure (identity, payments, logistics) that enables productive workflow enactment; and (iii) mobilizing trust-propagation mechanisms, including diaspora-linked financial and informational circuits. The model predicts that focusing on a minimum critical mass (~10–30%) of capable institutions generates higher marginal social returns than strategies emphasizing broad, individual-level diffusion. Conceptually, MED reorients AI-for-development strategy toward threshold-sensitive, institution-first deployment pathways, offering a tractable basis for reconceptualizing readiness metrics, policy priorities, and capital-allocation heuristics in LLMIC settings.

title: The Great Bitcoin Debate: Saylor's Maximalism Versus Schiff's Monetary Traditionalism

detail.title: The Great Bitcoin Debate: Saylor's Maximalism Versus Schiff's Monetary Traditionalism
detail.abstract: This paper examines the contemporary debate between Bitcoin maximalism and traditional monetary economics through the lens of the public disagreement between Strategy (formerly MicroStrategy) Executive Chairman Michael Saylor and economist Peter Schiff. Their dispute represents a fundamental clash over theories of value, monetary legitimacy, and prudent corporate financial strategy. Saylor's transformation of Strategy into a leveraged Bitcoin acquisition vehicle embodies the thesis that Bitcoin represents superior digital capital with mathematical scarcity advantages over fiat currency and traditional stores of value. Schiff's critique characterizes this approach as a potentially fraudulent Ponzi scheme reliant on unsustainable debt issuance and speculative appreciation. This paper analyzes the theoretical foundations underlying each position, examines the empirical evidence regarding Strategy's controversial corporate strategy, and evaluates the academic and financial literature addressing Bitcoin's dual nature as both a speculative asset and potential store of value. The analysis reveals that while Bitcoin exhibits characteristics consistent with both interpretations, Strategy's leveraged implementation creates significant structural vulnerabilities that validate core concerns raised by monetary traditionalists.

detail.abstract: What happens when the soil that supports the livelihoods of farmers is disturbed by the pursuit of gold beneath it, and farmers are compelled to adapt to survive? Such is the case for artisanal and small-scale mining (ASM) in Ghana, where race for gold is reshaping rural landscapes and pushing farm households into a struggle for survival over scarce resources like land, water and labor. ASM has led to severe destruction of farmlands and water bodies, negatively impacting the livelihoods of farm households that are already grappling with climate-induced shocks. This study investigates the adoption of coping strategies to mitigate the negative impacts of ASM by 316 farmers in the Ahafo Region of Ghana. The study uses descriptive statistics and a multivariate probit (MVP) model to identify and analyze demographic, socioeconomic , and institutional drivers of the adoption of different coping strategies. Evidence suggests that farmers use coping strategies as either substitutes or complements, demonstrating intricate decision-making shaped diverse factors. The study advocates for robust farmer groups, credit system and extension services to enhance farmers' resilience. The results augment empirical studies on livelihood adaptation and resilience in mining areas and provide policy-relevant insights for sustainable rural development.

detail.abstract:
The relationship between humans and the environment has been discussed and investigated from different points of view. Many jurists disagree about whether this relationship can be examined from a legal point of view, and some even go so far as to refer to international environmental law (IEL) as global ethics. But looking at the formation and development of IEL in the last decades, it becomes clear that this field, as one of the branches of public international law, has been able to include principles and rules. Since the environment has no boundaries and all humanity is on a single ship called the Earth, any damage to this ship will cause the destruction and decay of the entire human society. In the shadow of the development and expansion of this legal field, the right to a healthy environment, the common heritage of humanity, the rights of future generations, and the right to development were crystallized as examples of environmental rights.

title: Nonparametric Time-Varying Local Projections

detail.title: Nonparametric Time-Varying Local Projections
detail.abstract: Local projections are widely used to estimate impulse response functions, yet there is substantial evidence that these responses change over time in many macroeconomic and financial settings. To better capture such dynamics, we adopt a nonparametric time-varying local projection framework and estimate the coefficients using local linear regression. Our approach is agnostic to the source of time variation and imposes minimal structure on the underlying data-generating process, making it suitable for analyzing macroeconomic and financial series with model uncertainty. To accommodate flexible temporal dependence and heavy-tailed distributions, we adopt the τ-mixing framework and develop a computationally tractable estimator for the long-run variance that can be an alternative to standard HAC corrections. In high-dimensional settings with a large number of controls, we incorporate a post-double selection lasso procedure to address model selection uncertainty and enable uniformly valid inference. Simulation studies demonstrate strong finite-sample performance, and an empirical application to severe weather shocks reveals significant departures from estimates obtained using parameterized nonlinear VARs. Our results highlight the advantages of a flexible, data-driven strategy for characterizing dynamic responses in complex economic environments.

title: Polyvalent Decision Theory
affiliations: Université Paris I Panthéon-Sorbonne - Centre d'Economie de la Sorbonne (CES)

detail.title: Polyvalent Decision Theory
detail.abstract: A single agent may encounter many sources of uncertainty and many menus of outcomes, which can be combined together into many different decision problems. There may be analogies between different uncertainty sources (or different outcome menus). Some uncertainty sources (or outcome menus) may exhibit internal symmetries. The agent may also have different levels of awareness. In some situations, the state spaces and outcome spaces have additional mathematical structure (e.g. a topology or differentiable structure), and feasible acts must respect this structure (i.e. they must be continuous or differentiable functions). In other situations, the agent might only be aware of a set of abstract "acts", and be unable to specify explicit state spaces and outcome spaces. We introduce a new approach to decision theory that addresses these issues. It posits multiple uncertainty sources and outcome menus, linked by the aforementioned analogies, symmetries, and awareness changes. It makes no assumption about the internal structure of these sources and menus, so it is applicable in diverse mathematical environments (i.e. categories). In this framework, we define a suitable notion of subjective expected utility (SEU) representations, and provide conditions under which such SEU representations are unique.

title: Mastering Variance in Individualized Mixed-Model Assemblies: Why the Variable Takt Outperforms the Fixed Takt
affiliations: WHU - Otto Beisheim School of Management and WHU - Otto Beisheim School of Management

detail.title: Mastering Variance in Individualized Mixed-Model Assemblies: Why the Variable Takt Outperforms the Fixed Takt
detail.abstract: Demands on assembly lines have increased rapidly owing to product individualization and technology innovation, causing variance in processing times both locally (across product variants at a single line station) and globally (across products for the entire line). Manufacturers address such variance either by increasing a fixed maximum takt or by adopting a fixed weighted-average takt time (WATT) with repetitive Heijunka lots. The former approach entails severe takt time losses; the latter, complex and inflexible production planning. We offer a holistic and fundamentally different approach (using T-Bars and permissible overwork, among other things) to mastering variance-one that is simple, efficient, and flexible. Thus, we demonstrate that for mastering local variance, innovative and practice-proven levers (e.g., circular assemblies and parallel stations), which explicitly address processing times that exceed the takt time, offer a flexible and compelling alternative to classical levers (i.e., feeding lines and floaters). Global variance is mastered by stipulating product-specific takt times, which enable an arbitrary sequence of (individualized) products to be launched onto the line. Under very general assumptions, we prove that the variable takt strictly outperforms the fixed takt and that increasing product individualization can be handled much more efficiently by a variable takt than a fixed takt. We show that assembly lines can be designed to realize the shortest delivery lead time while achieving a resource-efficient line balance even for highly individualized products. A fixed takt system constrains companies' customer-driven focus and, moreover, accepts unbalanced workloads as a given. Adopting a variable takt allows companies to benefit from eliminating takt time losses, reducing worker stress, and overcoming limits on product individualization.

This paper refrains from making factual determinations regarding online allegations against any specific individuals or institutions. Instead, it adopts a ‘systemic security governance’ methodology to explore how the legislature can achieve risk containment, factual clarification, and institutional consolidation within the rule of law framework when significant societal doubts arise (including ‘indications of potential external undue influence during the legislative proposal stage’) and supporting regulations have yet to form a rigid closed-loop system. detail.abstract: Purpose-This study explores how self-initiated expatriates (SIEs) construct and manage their careers in a culturally and institutionally distinct host country context. Drawing on protean and boundaryless career theory, the study investigates the career barriers faced by SIEs, the strategies they employ to manage them, and how gender shapes these experiences. Design/methodology/approach-The study adopts a qualitative, inductive approach based on semi-structured interviews with European SIEs working in Japan. The data was analysed using the Gioia methodology to code, review, and organize the data systematically. Findings-Participants described structural exclusion, cultural misalignment, and institutional inflexibility as key constraints. In response, they pursued proactive, boundaryless, and valuesdriven strategies, including networking, skill development, and career recalibration. Female SIEs experienced a dual outsider status and had to perform identity work to gain legitimacy in maledominated environments. Originality-This study contributes to global career theory by examining how SIEs construct careers under constraint, introducing the concept of anchored boundaryless careers, and highlighting the intersection of gender and foreignness in shaping expatriate trajectories within structurally complex and culturally unique labour markets.

title: Cost Reduction Strategies in United States Infrastructure Projects: An Empirical Assessment of Planning, Procurement, and Lifecycle Efficiency
affiliations: Ain Shams University Cairo

detail.title: Cost Reduction Strategies in United States Infrastructure Projects: An Empirical Assessment of Planning, Procurement, and Lifecycle Efficiency

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there is no conflict of interest associated with the development, analysis or presentation of the research. No personal, financial or organizational interest influenced the interpretation of findings or the preparation of the manuscript.
declarations.funderStatement: The research received no external funding. All work associated with data collection, analysis and manuscript preparation was completed without financial support from donors, organizations or funding bodies.

detail.abstract: Regardless of the improved regulatory policies and the growing involvement of the public in infrastructure development in the United States, the issue of cost overruns remains constant. This research represents an empirical evaluation of the various methods of reducing costs based on the overall impact of planning efficiency, procurement strategy, and lifecycle cost management on project cost performance. A structured survey on 100 infrastructure professionals working on publicly funded projects in transportation, utilities, energy, and public facilities was utilized as primary data collection through a quantitative, cross-sectional research design. To test three hypotheses of planning, procurement, and lifecycle practices, the use of the statistical tests of reliability, regression, analysis of variance, and t-tests was used. The results indicate that the determinant that has the most effect on cost performance is the planning efficiency. Quality early cost estimation, scope definition, systematic risk identification, regulatory preparedness, as well as suitable contingency allocation are all considerably related to better cost results. Value-based selection, technical quality, early contractor involvement, and collaborative practices, which are a great part of the procurement strategies, are also closely associated with less cost overrun when compared with the traditional lowest price-oriented procurement models. Conversely, the lifecycle cost management practices demonstrate weak and statistically unimportant associations with long-term cost efficiency, although they are moderately aware of their importance. The findings demonstrate that cost overruns in the infrastructure development projects in the United States are dependent on the initial stage decisions incorporated in planning and procurement, and not on the downstream lifecycle factors. The research is valuable to the literature because it provides a comprehensive empirical framework that is specific to the context of the United States. In practical terms, the results point to enhanced capabilities of front-end planning, procurement transformation to value-based approaches, and institutionalization of lifecycle thinking to deliver sustainable and quantifiable cost savings in infrastructure delivery.

title: Moving Money Around: Mobile Energy Storage and the Value of Geospatial Flexibility
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania - The Wharton School, Harvard University - Technology & Operations Management Unit and University of Pennsylvania - The Wharton School

detail.title: Moving Money Around: Mobile Energy Storage and the Value of Geospatial Flexibility
detail.abstract: The growth of renewable energy has intensified the need for solutions that can address temporal and spatial mismatches between electricity supply and demand, arising from the intermittency of renewables. While battery storage has emerged as a key tool to store renewable electricity for future use, storage developers face diminishing and uncertain returns. In this paper, we first demonstrate how local competition and transient transmission capacity congestion lead to low and uncertain returns for Stationary Energy Storage System (SESS) operators. Using six years of price data from the PJM Interconnection and a staggered diff-in-diff approach, we estimate that an additional storage installation reduces existing SESS's annual profit at that location by $7,820 per megawatt on average. We then estimate how Mobile Energy Storage Systems (MESS)—an innovative business model that allows grid-scale batteries to be relocated—can increase operators' returns and improve grid-level congestion by providing geospatial flexibility. We introduce a dynamic programming-based forecasting framework for MESS developers' relocation and operating decisions and show that, even when relocation costs are high, MESS's profit consistently outperforms even the best-sited SESS by 11-47%. In part, this profit increase is driven by MESS capturing up to 22.5% more value from congestion prices than SESS, better aligning developer and grid incentives. Our findings quantify how competition and transience of price patterns limit storage profitability and highlight how leveraging mobile storage inventory in the energy transition can help storage developers, grid planners, and policymakers to accelerate storage build-out, renewable integration, and grid flexibility.

title: Critical Competencies for Government Affairs Managers: Insights From a Delphi Study
affiliations: Yonsei University and Yonsei University

detail.title: Critical Competencies for Government Affairs Managers: Insights From a Delphi Study
detail.abstract: Technology firms increasingly operate where public and private sectors intersect, heightening the importance of government affairs professionals who navigate complex regulations and relationships. This study uses a three-phase Delphi method, drawing on a final panel of 25 expert panelists from leading technology companies, to identify essential knowledge, skills, and abilities (KSAs) for senior government affairs managers. High-consensus KSAs include Stakeholder Management, Ethics and Integrity, Political Acumen, and Networking and Diplomacy, underscoring the strategic nature of these roles. The resulting framework can guide professional development, recruitment, and training. It also highlights ethical responsibilities, emphasizing trust-building with regulators and society. Future work could explore how these KSAs vary by region or organizational context. Overall, the study offers a practical resource to support effective public-private collaboration and addresses a growing demand for more structured competency models in government relations.

title: The Pricing of Stock Uncertainty under Short-Sale Constraints in China Stock Market
affiliations: Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU) - Shanghai Advanced Institute of Finance (SAIF), Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU), Antai College of Economics and Management, Students, Business School, National University of Singapore and Independent

detail.title: The Pricing of Stock Uncertainty under Short-Sale Constraints in China Stock Market
detail.abstract: This paper examines the pricing of stock uncertainty in the Chinese stock market, where short-sale constraints are nearly binding. We introduce the absolute value of the macro-finance uncertainty beta as a novel measure of stock uncertainty and document a significantly negative uncertainty premium, which is more pronounced among stocks with high information asymmetry. These findings suggest that the negative uncertainty premium reflects mispricing and market inefficiencies induced by short-sale restrictions, consistent with the implications of Miller (1977). Accordingly, relaxing short-sale constraints and improving market design could enhance stock market efficiency, resource allocation, and promote economic growth in China.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Algorithmic Pricing in Practice: Machine Learning Methods and Antitrust Implications

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence and Algorithmic Pricing in Practice: Machine Learning Methods and Antitrust Implications
detail.abstract: Algorithmic pricing has emerged as the digital weapon in a world in which antitrust enforcement risks following statutory guidelines crafted for an analog age. This observation does not imply that existing antitrust laws do not address the role of algorithmic pricing in anticompetitive conduct arising from horizontal, vertical, or hub-and-spoke agreements. Rather, it reflects acknowledgment that technological advancement now affords anticompetitive conduct a greater degree of camouflage that strains detection through traditional antitrust methods. 2 As this essay discusses, algorithmic tacit collusion has the potential to render stalwart antitrust defenses against explicit coordination little more than a Maginot Line in industries that have adopted algorithmic pricing as well as the potential to create an adverse selection problem that drives out potentially beneficial applications. 3. This essay addresses three main applications of such pricing: price discrimination, rivals using different algorithm providers, and rivals using the same algorithmic provider, with examples of use on E-commerce platforms such as Amazon and Walmart, airlines, real estate, and hospitality industries. Concurrently, this essay addresses the role of anchoring on acceptance and rejection of pricing recommendations. Next, in an effort to "demystify" algorithms such as Qlearning, neural networks, random forests and others, this essay offers an accessible introduction to these algorithms and their applications. In each case, this essay discusses the key inputs and likely outputs of interest from these algorithms for legal practitioners and regulators. This essay concludes with an overview of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) which consists of various methods that attempt to offer insight into black-box pricing algorithms.

title: Hybrid Justice Model (HJM): A Unified Framework for Fairness, Stability, and Governance in UN Recruitment

detail.title: Hybrid Justice Model (HJM): A Unified Framework for Fairness, Stability, and Governance in UN Recruitment

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly used in public-sector recruitment, yet statistical fairness alone cannot guarantee perceived fairness-especially in multicultural, politically sensitive institutions such as the United Nations. This paper develops the Hybrid Justice Model (HJM), a unified framework integrating algorithmic fairness, organizational justice, attribution-based perception dynamics, and stability modelling. The model introduces six components: AI fairness (F), human fairness (H), the Fairness Gap Index (FGI), the Justice Gap Index (JGI), the Perception Shift Index (PSI), and the λ-μ dynamic stability equation. Together, these components quantify misalignment between technical and experiential fairness, track trust trajectories over time, and evaluate whether correction-reaction cycles remain stable or become oscillatory. The methodology operationalizes each indicator using standardized fairness metrics, justice-dimension surveys, behavioral reaction data, and UN governance requirements. Applying the model to UN recruitment reveals four structural risks-perceptual opacity, overcorrection loops, silent trust erosion, and region-specific fairness gaps. The paper presents a three-phase implementation roadmap including baseline diagnostics, pilot deployment, and institutional integration aligned with UNGA A/RES/78/265 and the CEB AI Model Policy. HJM offers a governance-ready architecture that enables the UN to monitor fairness continuously, calibrate corrections dynamically, and strengthen legitimacy in an era where trust is increasingly fragile.

title: Adaptive Merit Framework: Merit-Anchored Fairness via SES Correction
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Adaptive Merit Framework: Merit-Anchored Fairness via SES Correction

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal, financial, or organizational conflicts of interest related to this research. This study was conducted independently without external influence.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this study as it uses publicly available, anonymized PISA data and synthetic simulation data. No human participants or identifiable personal information were involved.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The study was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: College admissions systems worldwide continue to face a structural tension between meritocracy and equity. Conventional fairness interventions-affirmative action, categorical quotas, and proxy-based targetingoften rely on coarse indicators (e.g., race or region), operate within fixed quotas that induce zero-sum tradeoffs, and lack transparent decision rules. This paper introduces the Adaptive Merit Framework (AMF), a policy-engineered mechanism that recognizes latent potential while preserving merit-based thresholds. AMF integrates three components: (1) a merit-anchored architecture in which conditional admits must exceed the same threshold as regular admits, (2) a dynamic threshold anchored to the raw score of the last regular admit, and (3) direct, continuous SES measurement verified through administrative data. Empirical validation using the full PISA 2022 Korea dataset (N=6,377) shows that AMF identifies 4, 6, and 9 additional admits under α = 5, 10, and 15 respectively (0.06-0.14% of cohort). Population-weighted estimates using OECD sampling weights suggest that the real-world scale of conditional admits is modestly larger than the raw sample counts, yielding approximately 491, 603, and 760 additional admits under α = 5, 10, and 15. All conditional admits exceed the merit threshold by 0.16 to 6.14 points, indicating that AMF recognizes suppressed performance rather than relaxing standards. Beyond SES-based corrections, AMF provides a design template for unified admissions architectures that replace fragmented equity tracks and support multi-dimensional evaluation frameworks. The correction rule M * i = M i + α • (0.5-S i) is compatible with any composite metric M i , enabling gradual transitions from single-metric evaluations to more diversified, transparent assessment systems.

title: The Effect of Green Energy, and Innovation on Green Growth: Insight from BRICS Countries
affiliations: Sakarya University - Department of Economics and University of Florida

detail.title: The Effect of Green Energy, and Innovation on Green Growth: Insight from BRICS Countries
detail.abstract: This study examines how green energy and technological innovation shape green growth in the BRICS economies over 1990-2021. We construct a green growth indicator that adjusts GDP per capita for environmental damages and education expenditure and estimate method-of-moments quantile regressions that account for cross-sectional dependence, non-normality, and heterogeneity. The results show that both renewable energy use and innovation significantly and positively affect green growth across the entire conditional distribution, with the largest effects at higher quantiles and for innovation. Financial development supports green growth mainly in low-performing countries, whereas trade openness exerts a small but generally negative effect. An expanding labor force is associated with lower green growth, consistent with reliance on resource-and laborintensive production. Our findings underscore the importance of scaling up renewable-energy deployment and innovation policy, while redirecting trade, finance, and labor-demand structures toward cleaner, more productivity-enhancing activities in emerging economies in BRICS and similar emerging economies.

detail.abstract: This article examines how energy access in low-resource and poverty settings is shaped by interconnected economic, infrastructural, social, and governance determinants, and how decentralised renewable options can respond when implemented through community-based approaches. It reviews conceptual ambiguities of "energy community" and argues that, in marginalised and low-resource contexts, goals are often defined less by market participation than by poverty reduction, productive uses of energy, and social development. Using three community-based initiatives in Mayotte-a Clean Mobility, a Social Housing and a Collective Interest energy community-the paper analyses participation and empowerment, inclusion and recognition justice, and contextualisation through a socio-ecological systems lens. Findings highlight that effective initiatives align technology with everyday practices, build bridging and bonding social capital, and adapt governance, tariffs, and partnerships to local institutions and constraints. The article concludes by outlining cornerstones for designing resilient, equitable grassroots energy communities under conditions of poverty, informality, and climate risk over time.

title: Immigration Enforcement And The Major Questions Doctrine
affiliations: Pace University - School of Law

detail.title: Immigration Enforcement And The Major Questions Doctrine

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No financial relationship.

detail.abstract:
This Article harnesses a doctrine traditionally central to conservative causes and jurisprudence to challenge a new instrument in the Trump Administration’s immigration enforcement regime. Specifically, it examines the Department of Homeland Security (DHS)’s reliance on the Alien Registration Act of 1940 in creating a universal immigrant registration that imposes strict criminal liabilities for noncompliance. This Article contends that the agency’s implementation amounts to unheralded and transformative regulatory rulemaking that runs afoul of the Supreme Court’s “major questions doctrine.” By leveraging registration requirements to effect sweeping policy and enforcement outcomes, DHS asserted authority of vast economic and political significance without clear congressional authorization. As such, courts should invalidate it.

The Article makes a number of unique contributions. It situates the Alien Registration Requirement within a broader expansion of executive power; it identifies the constitutional tensions that arise when executive agencies convert ancillary statutory mechanisms into primary enforcement tools; and it explains why the asserted authority exceeds permissible interpretive bounds.

Additionally, it creates a litigation strategy that, if successful, could serve as a model to confront an increasingly authoritarian Executive. Curtailing DHS’ rapid rulemaking serves the additional purpose of forcing Congress to speak explicitly on whether a universal registration (and extreme targeting and punishment of immigrants through the same) is the will of the people.

title: Robust Median Voter Rules
affiliations: University of Graz and Dalhousie University

detail.title: Robust Median Voter Rules
detail.abstract: Generalized median voter (GMV) rules on the single-peaked preference domain are group strategy-proof. We show that if incomplete information coexists with the ability to commit to coalitional agreements, then GMV rules can be susceptible to insincere voting by groups with heterogeneous beliefs. We identify strategic compromise as a novel source of insincere voting in this environment. Our two main results characterize the set of fair, efficient, and robust voting rules: those that ensure sincere voting under asymmetric information and coalition formation. Each result uses a different notion of robustness, and both give (at most) two alternatives special treatment, with the remaining alternatives chosen according to a type of consensus.

title: The Competition for India's Antitrust Jurisdiction: Competition Commission Versus Sectoral Regulators

detail.title: The Competition for India's Antitrust Jurisdiction: Competition Commission Versus Sectoral Regulators
detail.abstract: A string of judgments by Indian courts have downgraded the Competition Commission of India’s position in the adjudicatory hierarchy by requiring it to await the findings of sectoral regulators before initiating its own investigation. This article argues that the reasons advanced for deferring the Commission’s jurisdiction are erroneous. Further, the judicial test for deferral of the Commission’s jurisdiction is fraught with deficiencies and would inordinately delay or de facto divest the Commission of its jurisdiction. Some recent cases are trying to break away from this trend. One final battle though remains to be fought. With the emergence of competition issues in data protection and privacy related cases and the imminent establishment of data regulator(s) in India, the Commission will soon have an opportunity to push courts to re-examine and re-interpret existing judicial principles and reclaim its relative position in the adjudicatory hierarchy.

title: Group Boycotts and Free Speech: The Intersection of Antitrust and the First Amendment

detail.title: Group Boycotts and Free Speech: The Intersection of Antitrust and the First Amendment
detail.abstract: This article examines the legal tension between antitrust law and the First Amendment through recent advertiser boycotts of X (formerly Twitter) and related disputes in the media industry. It traces the evolution of U.S. group boycott doctrine to show how courts have struggled to distinguish between economic and political boycotts. The paper argues that this binary framework is increasingly inadequate in an era when collective refusals to deal often mix economic and expressive motivations.

title: The multiverse across asset classes: Design uncertainty in asset allocations
affiliations: HSBC Global Asset Management, HEC Paris - Finance Department, EMLYON Business School and HSBC Global Asset Management

detail.title: The multiverse across asset classes: Design uncertainty in asset allocations
detail.abstract: This paper documents the performance sensitivity of asset allocation methods with respect to design choices in the backtests. Endowed with five asset classes, we document the variations in Sharpe ratio of strategies with alternative (i) utility functions, (ii) signal-generating algorithms, (iii) sample periods, (iv) rebalancing frequency and (v) leeway with respect to a given benchmark, i.e, tracking error constraints. Our results show that while risk aversion does not impact risk-adjusted performance much (risk and return vary together), all other options can either significantly boost or deteriorate Sharpe ratios, especially signal source and inception date. Standard machine learning predictions nevertheless appear to deliver superior performance in a large majority of empirical designs.
